name: Brutalism
summary: Heavy masses of board-marked concrete with the structure, the services and the circulation shown on the outside. It grew from Le Corbusier's late work and from British post-war housing, and it built the universities and town halls of the welfare state.

philosophy.core_thesis: A building is honest when its material, its structure and its use are legible from the street.
design_principles: Leave the primary material unfinished: cast concrete keeps the marks of its timber formwork, and brick stays unrendered.
Show the structure: express frames, cross-walls, beams and cantilevers as the main image of the facade.
Compose with a few large repeated masses, and let each mass state one function such as a stair tower or an auditorium.
Set windows deep in the wall, at least 300mm behind the face, so that shadow and not glass draws the elevation.
Put services, stair cores and walkways on the outside of the volume where a visitor can read them.
Use one dominant material for more than 70% of the visible surface.
anti_patterns: Smooth render, paint or cladding panels over the concrete
Curtain walls of flush glass that hide the floor slabs
Applied ornament, mouldings or historical motifs
Thin, light profiles that make the building look weightless
A hidden entrance or a structure that cannot be read from outside
Bright decorative colour on the primary mass

massing.form: Blocky interlocked volumes with deep cantilevers and top-heavy silhouettes; the upper floors often project 2 to 6m beyond the base.
massing.proportion: Horizontal bands dominate, and vertical stair or service towers punctuate them at regular intervals.
massing.roof: Flat roofs with heavy parapets; plant rooms and lift overruns stand as sculpted volumes on top.
massing.relation_to_ground: The mass sits on pilotis, a podium or a raised deck, and ramps or bridges carry pedestrians above the street.

structure.system: In-situ reinforced concrete frames and cross-walls, with precast panels on later and larger schemes.
structure.span_and_module: A repeated structural bay of 3 to 7m sets the rhythm of the facade and the size of each room.
structure.expression: Beams, columns, corbels and waffle slabs stay visible inside and outside, and joints between pours are drawn as lines.

materials.finish: Unfinished and matt; the surface keeps formwork grain, tie holes and weather stains, and nothing is polished or painted.

palette.name: Signal orange
palette.role: small accents on doors and signs

facade.composition: A deep relief of repeated modules such as egg-crate grids, projecting window boxes or ribbed panels, without a decorative skin.
facade.openings: Recessed strip or punched windows in dark frames, shaded by concrete fins or brise-soleil.
facade.solid_to_void: Solid dominates: 60–80% of the elevation is opaque wall.

light_and_space.daylight: Light arrives from clerestories, deep slots and rooflights, and rakes across rough surfaces to show their texture.
light_and_space.spatial_sequence: A low compressed entrance opens to a tall central hall; ramps, bridges and open stairs make the route a visible event.
light_and_space.interior_character: The interior repeats the exterior materials: exposed concrete soffits, brick floors, built-in timber benches and little applied finish.

ornament.attitude: No applied ornament; the texture of the formwork and the pattern of the structure do the work of decoration.

rules.rule: Make the mass large and heavy, and show it.
Repeat the cast bay of the concrete form as a strong beat.
Set rough concrete against deep shadow and a few openings.
Stack the blocks into a stepped, cliff-like group.
Link the blocks by walkways and bridges that show the route.

emotion.target_response: Weight and permanence: the viewer feels a civic institution that will not move and has nothing to hide.

avoid_when: The brief asks for lightness, transparency or a domestic welcome.
The climate is wet and the budget has no allowance for concrete detailing that sheds water.

modifiers.how: Thin the frame, raise the glazing share above 50% and smooth the concrete; keep the flat roof and the repeated module.

sources.title: Reyner Banham, The New Brutalism: Ethic or Aesthetic? (Architectural Press, 1966)
